title: Investment: Aware Super warns of runaway AI hype after float collapse
full_text:
One of the country's largest super funds says it wants to give members more exposure to the AI boom but that it will not invest in companies with untested plans after the collapse of Firmus' sharemarket float.
Aware Super's head of public equities, Agnes Hong, whose fund manages more than $240 billion in assets, said, "We're backers of AI but not believers in blind faith."
"Many of these companies have ambitious growth targets, and they'll need to meet them or risk disappointing the market," said Hong. "We expect AI to lift productivity over time, but the potential has to turn into returns.
"We're discerning about where we allocate ... we want exposure spread across the theme, not concentrated in a single bet, and if concentration passes a sensible threshold, we're prepared to reduce our exposure."
While not a specific reference to Firmus, the comments shed light on the broader $4.7 trillion retirement sector's decision to stay out of the most heavily hyped ASX float in years.
Hong would not comment on Aware's exposure to Firmus, but sources briefed on the matter said that Australian Retirement Trust and UniSuper passed on opportunities to invest in the initial public offering.
NGS Super chief investment officer Ben Squires, who manages an $18 billion portfolio and also passed on the IPO, characterised an investment in Firmus at this stage as a "leap of faith".
Firmus was initially pitched at a $43 billion valuation with an $11 per share offer price, but bankers were scrambling to fill significant gaps in its bookbuild on Wednesday night and Thursday morning.
The syndicate was offering shares as low as $8.25, cutting billions of dollars from the IPO, before a long period of radio silence on Thursday left the entire deal in the balance and, on Friday morning, the float was pulled.
Backed by semiconductor maker Nvidia, Blackstone and high-profile local fund managers such as Wilson Asset Management and Regal Funds Management, Firmus plans to build data centres throughout Asia with top-of-the-line Nvidia chips and rent out the compute power to the likes of Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and other AI developers.
Central to the pitch is its proprietary cooling technology that Firmus said allowed it to run the quickly depreciating chips faster and for longer than other data centres. But even this was questioned of late after it emerged a failure in this system had flooded a data centre operated by the business's former partner, CDC Data Centres.
Hong said there was a genuine opportunity in the AI space, "but there's also hype, and we're watching valuations in some parts of the market very closely". "We've mapped our exposure across the whole portfolio rather than by asset class," she said. "Around 15 per cent of our high-growth option is in companies and assets directly tied to AI, and the true number is likely higher once those indirect links are counted."
